title: Courage Week 2 Equanimity
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: The talk explores the concept of equanimity, a key Buddhist teaching that refers to balance and composure in the face of challenges. It's not about ignoring or suppressing emotions, but rather about being fully present and attentive to what's happening, even when we're experiencing difficult feelings like grief. Equanimity is not something we achieve overnight, but rather it arises through consistent practice and mindfulness. By cultivating equanimity, we can develop the courage to ride the waves of life without getting overwhelmed or losing our sense of self, and we can respond with compassion and loving-kindness towards ourselves and others.
topics: don't set your heart on this

sentences.text: Just to recap, we left last week looking into the story of Mahapajapati and her requesting of the Buddha that women be ordained, and his response of "don't set your heart on this."
Our discussion today spent some time trying to ponder out exactly what that "don't set your heart on this" means.
There seems to be a lesson in grasping there, but is that adequate in the face of what seems to be a story whose values don't match ours, and yet a story that's core to our origination?
Eventually he is being talked by Ananda into relenting, as our story says, allowing women to be ordained at a subservient level.
Or maybe, if the current scholastic investigations are true, the subservience was tacked on later on.
Then we explored what courage is together, and I know more than one group found that, so last week we talked about how fear and courage are intertwined and there's some element of risk.
What came up today was that risk can be an overt risk of the body, or risk of exposing ourselves to others, or risk of exposing ourselves to ourselves.
In this exploration of courage we'd like to talk for a bit about the Buddhist tool of equanimity.
Equanimity, as our teaching goes, is balance in the presence of the storm.
We are barraged with arisings continuously.
Equanimity is neither clinging nor pushing away, and it's not something that we necessarily overtly do.
It's not magic.
Equanimity arises with and through our practice of sitting.
For years equanimity was mistranslated as indifference, which in a way is exactly opposite of what equanimity is.
Equanimity is being fully attentive to what's being thrown at us, not ignoring it. [unclear: "Winnie Nazarco"] has this great analogy of being like a master surfer.
The ocean of life is coming at us, and in moments when equanimity is present we're able to ride the waves, and those waves are changing fast.
It doesn't mean that we don't get wet, and we're not standing still or stopping the ocean.
Sometimes we slip off and we crash to the ground.
Equanimity doesn't mean we're not going to have emotions, [unclear: "imagine"] so there is grieving.
But what does it mean to fully and deeply grieve without losing our presence of mind?
Equanimity is also not suppression.

Sometimes in looking at gender, this is often associated with men but very much women too, there's a concept of dealing with things and being able to show how strong we are, when what we're kind of doing is just developing this really muscular anal sphincter muscle that squeezes all and holds all the crap inside.
That is not equanimity.

So in the story of Mahapajapati that we talked about today, when we talked about the gender difference, Mahapajapati was showing the Buddha that just sitting there and being logical and saying everything is fine doesn't really honestly cover the course of human life.
Maybe that's not what's important.
Equanimity includes that emotion.
One of our principal points in sitting is we say the liberation of all beings, and we know that that's not freedom from suffering but freedom in suffering.
So again, equanimity is not that we're sitting without the suffering.
We are sitting with the suffering immediately present, and the joy.
Buddha teaches about the two arrows.
Things happen to us, we have difficult events happen, and that's like being shot with an arrow.
Then we have a tendency to create our own stress on top of that arrow, and then maybe get mad at ourselves for creating stress on top of the arrow, and so it's like just shooting ourselves again.
Equanimity is the process of not taking a second arrow and sticking it in ourselves.
In the Buddhist teachings equanimity is not taught in isolation.
It's not something that we say, you just sit down and you don't get ruffled about stuff and you become equanimous.
Equanimity, among other lists, is taught in the four perfect immeasurables, the four Brahma Viharas, which are loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy and equanimity.
So where would equanimity be without that emotion in the compassion and the joy and the loving-kindness?
In fact it's listed last.

Sylvia Boorstein emphasizes that loving-kindness is natural to us: we see pain and we naturally respond with loving-kindness, just as part of our brain physiology, as we were talking about last time, as part of our limbic system.
Compassion is different from pity.
In compassion there's an empathy, there's a recognition that it's us too, it can be us.
Feeling that sympathetic joy is different than saying, "Well, I'm Buddhist and now everything is joy, I'm straight up happy," and expressing happiness blind to the pain that others are suffering.
That's again born out by science.
Babies, newborns very young, [unclear: "anyway take that down"] express distress on seeing the distress of others.
So let's take that tool of equanimity and be aware of it, and make the effort to be mindful with the joys and the sufferings that arise in ourselves and others.
Truly find the courage.
